--- title: "Python Polars: An Overview for tidyverse Users" subtitle: "Core concepts, the dplyr ↔ Polars Rosetta Stone, and common gotchas" jupyter: python3 --- # Introduction **Polars** is a DataFrame library for Python, written in Rust. Coming from the tidyverse, you will find it very familiar in spirit: it is the closest thing Python has to dplyr's *"verbs + column expressions"* style, but it runs on a multi-threaded, query-optimizing engine. ::: {.callout-note} ## Version This document targets **Polars 2.0**. The query syntax is the same as the 1.x series; the major changes in 2.0 are about *defaults* (most importantly, the lazy API now runs on the streaming engine, see @sec-lazy and @sec-gotchas). Older tutorials may still use pre-1.0 names such as `groupby` or `melt`, which no longer exist. ::: ::: {#a700331e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl pl.__version__ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` '2.0.0' ``` ::: ::: # The Core Mental Model Polars has only three ideas you need to internalize: ```text ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 1. DATA pl.DataFrame (eager) / pl.LazyFrame (lazy) │ │ │ │ 2. EXPRESSIONS "recipes" for computing a column │ │ pl.col("mass_g").mean().alias("avg_mass") │ │ ≈ tidy-eval: an unevaluated column computation │ │ │ │ 3. CONTEXTS the verbs that EVALUATE expressions │ │ select · with_columns · filter · group_by().agg │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Context (verb) Expression (what to compute) ┌────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ df.with_columns( │ ◄───── │ (pl.col("mass_g") / 1000) │ │ │ │ .alias("mass_kg") │ │ ) │ └───────────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────┘ ``` In dplyr, `mutate(mass_kg = mass_g / 1000)` uses **non-standard evaluation** (NSE), so you can write bare column names. Python has no NSE, so Polars makes the column reference explicit with `pl.col("mass_g")`. ::: {.callout-tip} ## The one-line translation rule `pl.col("x")` in Polars is the bare `x` in dplyr. Once that clicks, most dplyr code translates almost mechanically. ::: # Setup and a Toy Dataset ::: {#4a8d3112 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs # like tidyselect helpers df = pl.DataFrame({ "species": ["Adelie", "Adelie", "Gentoo", "Gentoo", "Chinstrap"], "island": ["Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Biscoe", "Biscoe", "Dream"], "bill_mm": [39.1, 37.8, 46.1, 50.0, 46.5], "mass_g": [3750, 3400, 4500, 5700, None], }) df # prints like a tibble: shape + dtypes are shown ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 4)
speciesislandbill_mmmass_g

"Adelie""Torgersen"39.13750
"Adelie""Biscoe"37.83400
"Gentoo""Biscoe"46.14500
"Gentoo""Biscoe"50.05700
"Chinstrap""Dream"46.5null
``` ::: ::: `glimpse()` works exactly like `dplyr::glimpse()`: ::: {#8fd6e4d2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 5 Columns: 4 $ species 'Adelie', 'Adelie', 'Gentoo', 'Gentoo', 'Chinstrap' $ island 'Torgersen', 'Biscoe', 'Biscoe', 'Biscoe', 'Dream' $ bill_mm 39.1, 37.8, 46.1, 50.0, 46.5 $ mass_g 3750, 3400, 4500, 5700, null ``` ::: ::: # The Rosetta Stone: dplyr ↔ Polars | tidyverse | Polars | |---|---| | `select(species, bill_mm)` | `df.select("species", "bill_mm")` | | `select(where(is.numeric))` | `df.select(cs.numeric())` | | `select(starts_with("b"))` | `df.select(cs.starts_with("b"))` | | `filter(mass_g > 4000)` | `df.filter(pl.col("mass_g") > 4000)` | | `mutate(kg = mass_g / 1000)` | `df.with_columns((pl.col("mass_g") / 1000).alias("kg"))` | | `rename(new = old)` | `df.rename({"old": "new"})` | | `arrange(desc(mass_g))` | `df.sort("mass_g", descending=True)` | | `group_by(x) |> summarise(...)` | `df.group_by("x").agg(...)` | | `group_by(x) |> mutate(...)` | `df.with_columns(expr.over("x"))` | | `n()` | `pl.len()` | | `distinct()` | `df.unique()` | | `slice_head(n = 3)` | `df.head(3)` | | `case_when()` / `if_else()` | `pl.when().then().otherwise()` | | `left_join(y, by = "k")` | `df.join(y, on="k", how="left")` | | `anti_join()` / `semi_join()` | `how="anti"` / `how="semi"` | | `pivot_wider()` | `df.pivot(on=..., index=..., values=...)` | | `pivot_longer()` | `df.unpivot(index=..., on=...)` | | `drop_na()` / `replace_na()` | `df.drop_nulls()` / `.fill_null(...)` | | `str_detect()` / `str_to_upper()` | `.str.contains()` / `.str.to_uppercase()` | | `lubridate::year()` | `.dt.year()` | | `|>` pipe | method chaining (wrapped in parentheses) | : Common tidyverse verbs and their Polars equivalents {.striped .hover} ## Quick examples ::: {#ac5ba6cf .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # select() with tidyselect-style helpers df.select(cs.numeric()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The outer parentheses let you break the chain across lines. This is the Polars equivalent of writing a `|>` pipeline. # Expressions: Where the Real Power Is An expression is a chain of operations on a column. It does nothing until a context runs it: ```text pl.col("bill_mm") ──► .fill_null(0) ──► .mean() ──► .round(1) ──► .alias("avg") (source) (transform) (aggregate) (transform) (name it) ``` ::: {#32506d30 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.select( pl.col("bill_mm").fill_null(0).mean().round(1).alias("avg") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Namespaces Related functions are grouped into namespaces, similar to how stringr, lubridate and purrr are organized in the tidyverse: ::: {#53fb6f64 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.col("species").str.to_lowercase() # .str ≈ stringr pl.col("date").dt.month() # .dt ≈ lubridate pl.col("tags").list.len() # .list ≈ list-columns / purrr pl.col("species").cast(pl.Categorical) # ≈ as.factor() ``` ::: ::: {#2a06f49d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.select( pl.col("species"), pl.col("species").str.to_uppercase().alias("upper"), pl.col("island").str.contains("^B").alias("starts_with_B"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Eager vs Lazy: The Big Performance Idea {#sec-lazy} This concept has no direct base-dplyr equivalent, but it works just like **dbplyr** and **duckplyr**: you describe the query first, then execute it. ```text EAGER (pl.DataFrame) LAZY (pl.LazyFrame) ─────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────── read_csv() → executes now scan_csv() → builds a plan only .filter() → executes now .filter() → adds to plan .group_by() → executes now .group_by() → adds to plan .collect() → optimize + execute ✓ The optimizer can: • push filters down into the file read • read only the needed columns • stream data in batches (> RAM) ``` A typical lazy pipeline over a file (not run here, since the file does not exist): ::: {#a8b67950 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} lazy_result = ( pl.scan_parquet("big_data.parquet") # nothing loaded yet .filter(pl.col("year") == 2025) .group_by("site") .agg(pl.len()) ) print(lazy_result.explain()) # inspect the optimized plan (≈ show_query()) df_out = lazy_result.collect() # execute (≈ collect() in dbplyr) ``` ::: Any eager DataFrame can be switched to lazy mode with `.lazy()`: ::: {#bb945442 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} lf = ( df.lazy() .filter(pl.col("mass_g").is_not_null()) .select("species", "mass_g") ) print(lf.explain()) # the query plan, before anything runs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` FILTER col("mass_g").is_not_null() FROM DF ["species", "island", "bill_mm", "mass_g"]; PROJECT["species", "mass_g"] 2/4 COLUMNS ``` ::: ::: Notice `PROJECT 2/4 COLUMNS` in the plan: the optimizer noticed that only two columns are needed and will read just those (**projection pushdown**). On a Parquet file with hundreds of columns, that saving is substantial. ::: {#dc28bc54 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} lf.collect() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

Since Polars 2.0, `.collect()` runs on the **streaming engine** by default, which processes data in batches and is typically faster and more memory efficient. ::: # Gotchas for tidyverse Users {#sec-gotchas} ## Columns in the same `with_columns()` can't see each other In `mutate(a = x + 1, b = a * 2)`, dplyr evaluates arguments sequentially. Polars runs all expressions in one context **in parallel**, so `b` cannot reference the brand-new `a`: ::: {#c034d6ba .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.with_columns( bill_cm = pl.col("bill_mm") / 10, bill_cm_x2 = pl.col("bill_cm") * 2, # bill_cm doesn't exist yet! ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

If you want the missing value preserved, handle it explicitly: ::: {#a3b23638 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.with_columns( size = pl.when(pl.col("mass_g").is_null()).then(None) .when(pl.col("mass_g") > 4000).then(pl.lit("big")) .otherwise(pl.lit("small")) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## Row order is not guaranteed unless you ask for it `group_by()` output order has never been guaranteed. Since Polars 2.0 (with the streaming engine as default), **joins and `unpivot()` may also return rows in a different order** than the input. If order matters, say so explicitly: ::: {#54748eb6 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg(...) # keep first-seen order df.join(other, on="k", how="left", maintain_order="left") # keep left order df.group_by("species").agg(...).sort("species") # or just sort ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} This change does **not** raise an error. A pipeline that silently relied on incidental row order (e.g. "left table order survives a left join") can produce differently ordered output after upgrading to 2.0. ::: ## `null` ≠ `NaN` `null` is R's `NA` (a missing value). `NaN` is a floating-point *not-a-number*. `drop_nulls()` does not remove `NaN`; use `fill_nan()` or `is_nan()` for those. ::: {#0e00c2b0 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = pl.DataFrame({"v": [1.0, None, float("nan")]}) x.with_columns( is_null = pl.col("v").is_null(), is_nan = pl.col("v").is_nan(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Strict types, no silent coercion Joining an `Int64` key to a `String` key raises an error instead of guessing. Use `.cast()` explicitly. This feels annoying at first, but it catches bugs early. ## No row names / index Unlike pandas, Polars has no index. Good news: tibbles don't have row names either, so your mental model carries over directly. ## Avoid `map_elements()` (row-wise Python functions) It is the equivalent of `rowwise()` plus a slow R function: it drops you out of the Rust engine and loses parallelism. There is almost always a native expression that does the same job. # Suggested Learning Path ```text Week 1: select / filter / with_columns / sort / group_by().agg (eager) Week 2: expressions deep dive: when/then, .over(), .str, .dt, selectors Week 3: joins, pivot/unpivot, nulls, dtypes & casting Week 4: lazy API: scan_*(), explain(), collect(), streaming large files ``` # Resources - Polars user guide: - Polars 2.0 upgrade guide: - API reference (Python): - Source code:
